description:
Matching a binary tail COPIED the remainder, so scanning n bytes copied the
whole tail at every step. Every byte scanner in the language was quadratic, and
no library could work around it because counting a run is itself a traversal.

THE COST IS IN BYTES COPIED, NOT ALLOCATIONS, and the counters could not see it.
The allocation COUNT is roughly linear -- about two per byte. What grew
quadratically was the bytes, and above SHARED_BIN_THRESHOLD_BYTES those bytes
are off-heap, where nothing counted them at all. The first before/after
measurement of the fix looked IDENTICAL for that reason: a ProcBin stub costs
the same whether its bytes were freshly copied or shared.

So the fix came with the measurement that makes it sayable --
`HeapAllocStats::shared_bin`, off-heap binary buffers, deliberately outside
`total` because they are not heap bytes and do not move under Cheney. With it,
off-heap bytes copied while decoding one JSON document:

     users  doc bytes   BEFORE      AFTER
         2         79     3,494          0
         8        247    94,560          0
        32        919 1,396,008          0

3.7x the input, 15x the copying, and a 919-byte document copied 1.4 MB. A bare
walk over 640 bytes went from 405,440 bytes copied to exactly 640, once.

FIXED (18c914a24): a ProcBin names a byte-aligned SUFFIX of a SharedBin, not the
whole thing. It carries a byte_offset and derives its length; the whole binary is
the suffix at offset 0. `<<_c, rest :: binary>>` asks for a suffix, so
fz_bs_read_field_bits hands back another view of the same bytes.

SUFFIX RATHER THAN AN ARBITRARY WINDOW IS LOAD-BEARING: every shared buffer
carries one invisible trailing NUL (fz-wu9), which is what lets a binary reach C
as a cstring without copying, and a suffix ends where the NUL is. So a window in
the middle is not constructible -- alloc_procbin takes an offset and DERIVES the
length -- and fz_binary_as_cstring needed no change.

Heap::alloc_bitstring_suffix makes the one decision: share above the threshold,
copy at or below it, where a copy is smaller than a stub and keeps a short tail
from pinning a long buffer alive.

A LIBRARY-LEVEL FIX WAS TRIED FIRST AND FALSIFIED: counting a run then taking
one slice measured WORSE (437 allocations vs 435), because counting the run is
itself the traversal. That is the evidence this was a data-model issue.

WHAT PINNING A SINGLE NUMBER WOULD HAVE COST: the epic's signal asked for an
allocation golden, and the obvious one was '435 allocations for a 68-byte
document'. Recording it would have enshrined the quadratic scan as correct. The
golden that landed instead (fz-5xp.17, json_decode_cost) pins a RATIO.

Also reframed fz-5xp.14: String is entirely byte scanning and would have been
quadratic before a line of it was written.

comments.text:
PARTIAL, and deliberately not the fix.

Extracting a binary field walked the source ONE BIT AT A TIME through a
BitWriter, even when the position and length were both byte-aligned -- which
every `<<c, rest :: binary>>` step over a binary is. That is now a slice copy:
8x less work per tail match, on the hottest path in any parser.

IT DOES NOT REDUCE ALLOCATIONS, and the counters confirm it: 21 allocations for
a 10-byte walk and 81 for 40, unchanged either way. The copy is smaller, not
absent.

The actual fix is still zero-copy slicing, which `fz_bs_read_field_bits` has
always deferred in a comment:

    // Build a fresh Bitstring from the slice. Always copy for v1
    // (zero-copy slicing deferred)

That needs a sub-binary object the GC understands -- it has to keep the parent
alive -- and a policy for when to flatten one back into a copy, which is the
usual space-leak trade in that design. `procbin` already carries some of the
machinery for a binary that points at bytes it does not own.

Recording the split because a change that moves no counter is exactly the kind
that gets mistaken later for having fixed the thing.

MEASUREMENT REFINED, and one claim in the description corrected.

Walking n bytes with `<<_c, r :: binary>>`:

     bytes | bitstring_allocs | bitstring_bytes | procbin_allocs
    -------|------------------|-----------------|---------------
        10 |               21 |             416 |             0
        40 |               81 |           2,880 |             0
       160 |              130 |           6,304 |           191
       320 |              130 |           6,304 |           511

The ALLOCATION COUNT is roughly LINEAR -- about two per byte, one for the
reader and one for the tail. My original description led with '435 allocations'
as though the count were the problem; it is not, and that framing was wrong.

What is quadratic is the BYTES COPIED: four times the input gives about seven
times the bitstring bytes, because each step copies the whole remainder.

And above SHARED_BIN_THRESHOLD_BYTES (64) the tails become PROCBINs, whose
shared bytes are allocated outside the process heap and do not appear in these
counters at all -- note bitstring_bytes flat at 6,304 from 160 to 320 while
procbin_allocs goes 191 to 511. So the copying cost at realistic input sizes is
WORSE than the process-heap counters suggest, not better, and a JSON document of
any size is entirely in that regime.

That also points at where the fix is cheapest: a sub-binary of a PROCBIN can
share the existing handle with a different offset and length, and the refcount
and MSO machinery for 'a binary that points at bytes it does not own' is already
there. Small inline bitstrings can keep copying -- under 64 bytes it does not
matter.

SUSPENDED, and the reason is worth recording precisely.

The design was: a ProcBin stops being 'the shared binary' and becomes a
byte-aligned SUFFIX of one, carrying a byte_offset. Suffix rather than an
arbitrary window is load-bearing, because a suffix ends where the buffer's
invisible trailing NUL is (fz-wu9), so fz_binary_as_cstring keeps working with
no flattening copy -- and a suffix is exactly what every byte scanner asks for.

IT WORKS, AND THE NUMBERS ARE THE POINT. Off-heap bytes copied while decoding
one JSON document, before and after:

     users  doc bytes   copied BEFORE   AFTER
         2         79           3,494       0
         8        247          94,560       0
        32        919       1,396,008       0

3.7x the input, 15x the copying -- and decoding a 919-byte document copied
1.4 MB. A bare walk over n bytes went from 405,440 bytes copied at n=640 to
exactly 640, copied once.

MEASUREMENT GAP FOUND AND CLOSED ON THE WAY. None of that was visible: a ProcBin
stub costs the same whether its bytes were freshly copied or shared, so the heap
counters could not tell copying from sharing, and the first A/B looked
IDENTICAL. HeapAllocStats gains `shared_bin` -- off-heap binary buffers,
deliberately outside `total` because they are not heap bytes -- surfaced as
:shared_bin_allocs / :shared_bin_bytes. That counter is what makes the table
above sayable, and it is what fz-5xp.17's allocation golden needs.

WHY IT IS NOT LANDING YET. Its fixture crashes on `run` -- and the crash turned
out NOT to be this change. It is fz-5xp.60: two matched binary literals over 64
bytes corrupt a ProcBin's shared pointer and SIGBUS at teardown, silently, on
the JIT door. Pre-existing, and invisible until fz-5xp.57 made a big binary
matchable at all.

I spent a long time believing the widened stub caused it, because writing to
stub+16 turned the silent SIGBUS into a loud alignment panic. It did not: the
same crash reproduces with the widening entirely absent. Recorded because the
false lead cost hours.

BLOCKED ON fz-5xp.60. The work is understood and measured; it should land as
written once the static-shared-binary defect is fixed.

title: Matching a binary tail COPIES it, so every byte scanner is quadratic
